name: production-2026-09
note: Observation shape from Q6, per-device row counts from Q3, timestamp spread from Q14, index weight from Q7 and Q7c. Key counts are a median and 95th percentile; catchment volumes and row ages are a median, 90th and 99th, interpolated rather than fitted because program encounters are not one population.

catchment_rows_per_user.note: Q3, from each user's most recent sync. A 370x spread between the median device and the 99th percentile. Reproduce the tail: a generator giving every user a typical catchment produces no heavy syncs, and the heavy tail is where the choke points are.

temporal_spread.note: Q14. Age of last_modified_date_time in days, and how often a row is edited after creation. Per table, because they differ sharply: three quarters of program encounters are edited and the median edit lands 32 days after creation, against 383 to 595 days elsewhere. That is the scheduled-visit pattern -- the row is created when a visit is scheduled and filled in when it happens. A generator writing each row once produces neither the edit volume nor the spread, and an incremental sync then returns nothing.

index_weight_per_row.note: Q7 and Q7c, normalised per row so a smaller generated dataset can be compared against production directly. GIN bytes per row is the check H5 calls the single most informative one: it falls out of how many distinct observation keys each row carries, which is what H3 says is most likely to be got wrong. A generated index an order of magnitude lighter per row means the cardinality is wrong, the index is cache-resident, and every push figure will be optimistic.

observation_concept_cardinality.note: Q6 found 5,623 distinct observation keys in program_encounter, but that spans all 986 organisations -- the query carries no organisation filter. A single bundle reaches a few hundred through its live form mappings, so this is compared per organisation against the bundle's own reachable set, not against the platform-wide figure.
